::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a library card and the staff room"}
With a library card you can borrow books and see your own borrowing list, but not anyone else's. Some doors (the staff room) need a staff badge, and showing a library card there gets a polite "no". And when you hand in a change-of-address form, the clerk copies only the address boxes, even if you also wrote "promote me to head librarian" in the margin.

Atlas needs the same three habits: **ownership** (your saved issues are yours), **roles** (admins add repositories), and **only accepting the fields a form lists**.
:::

## The problem

Lessons 4.7 to 4.10 answered "who are you?". Now every request has a signed-in user, and the next question is "what may this user do?". Getting it wrong is the most common serious security bug in web APIs: it heads the OWASP Top 10 (a widely used list of the most critical web application risks) as **Broken Access Control**.

Here are two versions of that bug, in a copy of Atlas with two plausible-looking changes:

- a route `GET /users/{user_id}/saved-issues` that lists any user's saved issues, because "the web page needs it", and checks only that the caller is signed in;
- a `PATCH /users/me` that accepts any JSON object and copies every key onto the user, because "it's more flexible than a schema".

Mallory, an ordinary user, runs a short script against it:

```text
== vulnerable copy
Mallory reads user 22's saved issues -> 200 [{"id":1,"repo":"pytorch/ignite","number":20,"title":"Support new metric",...}]
Mallory PATCHes role=admin -> 200 role is now admin
Mallory adds a repository -> 201 {"id":5,"full_name":"mallory/evil","indexed_at":null}
```

She read someone else's data by changing a number in the URL, then made herself an administrator with one field, then used her new powers. Every request carried a valid token; authentication worked perfectly. Authorisation didn't exist.

## Theory

### Many-to-many, again

First, the data. A user can save many issues, and an issue can be saved by many users: a **many-to-many** relationship. Lesson 3.4 modelled one already (issues and labels) with a **join table**: a table whose rows each link one of each. `saved_issues` has `(user_id, issue_id, saved_at)`, and its primary key is the pair, so the same issue can't be saved twice by the same user.

### Three kinds of authorisation check

- **Role-based**: "only admins may add repositories". Check the user's role.
- **Ownership-based**: "you may see only your own saved issues". The cleanest way is to put the owner into the query itself: `WHERE user_id = :me`. A row that isn't yours is simply not found. Better still, where possible, leave the id out of the URL entirely: `/users/me/saved-issues` has nothing to change.
- **Field-based**: "you may change your skills profile, not your role". The request schema (lesson 4.3) lists the fields a client may send, and refuses anything else.

The two attacks above have names:

- **IDOR** (Insecure Direct Object Reference): the server uses an id from the request to fetch an object without checking it belongs to the caller.
- **Mass assignment**: the server copies all fields of a request onto a stored object, so a client sets fields it was never meant to touch (`role`, `id`, `created_at`).

### Which status code?

| Status | Meaning | Atlas example |
|---|---|---|
| **401 Unauthorized** | "Who are you?" No valid credentials. | no token on `PUT /issues/1/saved` |
| **403 Forbidden** | "I know who you are, and you may not." | a non-admin calls `POST /repos` |
| **404 Not Found** | It doesn't exist, *or* you may not know it exists. | someone else's note (lesson 4.20) |

Why 404 for someone else's private data rather than 403? A 403 confirms the object exists, which leaks information: which ids are in use, how many there are. For per-user data, "not found" is the honest answer from the caller's point of view. GitHub does the same for private repositories.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  Q[request] --> T{valid token?}
  T -->|no| U[401]
  T -->|yes| S{body has only<br/>allowed fields?}
  S -->|no| V[422]
  S -->|yes| R{route needs admin?}
  R -->|yes, not admin| F[403]
  R -->|no, or admin| O{row belongs to user?}
  O -->|no| N[404]
  O -->|yes| OK[200 / 204]
```

### Idempotent saving with PUT

"Save issue 42" is naturally idempotent: saving it again should change nothing and still succeed. So it's `PUT /issues/42/saved`, and in SQL an insert that ignores conflicts: Postgres's `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. `DELETE /issues/42/saved` is idempotent too: deleting something already gone still leaves it gone. Both answer **204 No Content**: success, nothing to send back.

## In the project

### Red: the rules as tests

```python
def test_saving_is_idempotent_and_private(client: TestClient, session: Session) -> None:
    ids = store_numbers(session, [1, 2])
    ada = sign_up(client, "ada@example.com")
    grace = sign_up(client, "grace@example.com")

    assert client.put(f"/issues/{ids[2]}/saved", headers=ada).status_code == 204
    assert client.put(f"/issues/{ids[2]}/saved", headers=ada).status_code == 204

    ada_saved = client.get("/users/me/saved-issues", headers=ada).json()
    assert [issue["number"] for issue in ada_saved] == [2]
    assert client.get("/users/me/saved-issues", headers=grace).json() == []

    assert client.delete(f"/issues/{ids[2]}/saved", headers=ada).status_code == 204
    assert client.get("/users/me/saved-issues", headers=ada).json() == []


def test_only_admins_may_add_a_repository(client: TestClient, session: Session) -> None:
    learner = sign_up(client, "ada@example.com")
    admin = admin_headers(client, session)
    body = {"full_name": "pytorch/ignite"}

    forbidden = client.post("/repos", json=body, headers=learner)
    created = client.post("/repos", json=body, headers=admin)
    duplicate = client.post("/repos", json=body, headers=admin)

    assert forbidden.status_code == 403
    assert created.status_code == 201 and created.json()["full_name"] == "pytorch/ignite"
    assert duplicate.status_code == 409


def test_patch_cannot_change_the_role(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """Mass assignment (lesson 4.11): fields the schema doesn't list are refused, not ignored."""
    headers = sign_up(client, "mallory@example.com")

    response = client.patch("/users/me", json={"role": "admin"}, headers=headers)

    assert response.status_code == 422
    assert response.json()["error"]["details"][0]["location"] == ["body", "role"]
    me = client.get("/users/me", headers=headers)
    assert me.json()["role"] == "user"
```

`store_numbers` saves sample issues the way `atlas issues --save` does (lesson 3.8) and returns their ids; `admin_headers` signs up a user and sets their role to `admin` directly in the database through the test session, the way `atlas make-admin` would.

The last test is the interesting one. Lesson 4.3's `UserUpdate` schema only lists `skills_profile`, so Atlas was already safe from Mallory's PATCH, but run against it, the test fails:

```text
E       assert 200 == 422
E        +  where 200 = <Response [200 OK]>.status_code
```

Pydantic's default is to *ignore* fields a model doesn't list. Mallory's `"role"` was dropped, her role stayed `user`, and the answer was 200. Safe, but silent: a client that misspelled `skils_profile` would also get 200 and wonder why nothing changed, and an attack attempt looks exactly like success. Refusing unknown fields makes both visible.

### Green: refusing unknown fields

In `schemas.py`, one shared setting, applied to every *request* schema (`UserCreate`, `UserUpdate`, `RefreshRequest`, `RepoCreate`, and the note schemas of lesson 4.20):

```python
# Request bodies refuse fields they don't list. Silently ignoring them would hide client
# mistakes ("skils_profile") and attack attempts ("role": "admin", lesson 4.11) alike.
REQUEST_BODY = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")


class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    """PATCH body: a client sends only the fields it wants to change. ..."""

    model_config = REQUEST_BODY

    skills_profile: str = Field(default="", max_length=2000)
```

Response schemas don't need it: they're built by Atlas from its own objects.

```text
$ curl -s -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/users/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"role": "admin"}'
{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"The request is not valid","request_id":"f8b135f9207e43ea82fd4ce818c74ddf","details":[{"location":["body","role"],"message":"Extra inputs are not permitted"}]}}
```

### The join table

In `models.py`, a plain `Table` because it has no behaviour of its own:

```python
saved_issues = Table(
    "saved_issues",
    Base.metadata,
    Column("user_id", ForeignKey("users.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True),
    Column("issue_id", ForeignKey("issues.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True),
    Column("saved_at", DateTime(timezone=True), nullable=False, server_default=func.now()),
)
```

`ondelete="CASCADE"`: when a user or an issue is deleted, their saved rows go too (lesson 3.5).

### Saving and unsaving: ownership from the token

`routes/issues.py`:

```python
@router.put("/{issue_id}/saved", status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
def save_issue(issue_id: int, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> Response:
    """PUT is idempotent: saving an already-saved issue changes nothing and still succeeds."""
    get_issue_or_404(session, issue_id)
    session.execute(
        insert(saved_issues)
        .values(user_id=user.id, issue_id=issue_id)
        .on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=["user_id", "issue_id"])
    )
    session.commit()
    return Response(status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)


@router.delete("/{issue_id}/saved", status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
def unsave_issue(issue_id: int, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> Response:
    session.execute(
        delete(saved_issues).where(
            saved_issues.c.user_id == user.id, saved_issues.c.issue_id == issue_id
        )
    )
    session.commit()
    return Response(status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
```

`insert` here comes from `sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql`, which adds `on_conflict_do_nothing`. In both routes the user id comes from `CurrentUser`, the token, and never from the URL or body. There's no way to save or unsave an issue *for someone else*: the request has nowhere to say who that would be. `saved_issues.c.user_id` is how you refer to a column of a plain `Table` (`c` for columns).

### Listing: no id to tamper with

`routes/users.py`:

```python
@router.get("/me/saved-issues", response_model=list[IssueOut])
def list_saved_issues(user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> list[IssueOut]:
    statement = (
        select(Issue)
        .join(saved_issues, saved_issues.c.issue_id == Issue.id)
        .where(saved_issues.c.user_id == user.id)
        .order_by(saved_issues.c.saved_at.desc())
        # Load every issue's labels and repo in one extra query each, not one per issue (N+1).
        .options(selectinload(Issue.labels), selectinload(Issue.repo))
    )
    return [issue_out(issue) for issue in session.scalars(statement)]
```

Compare with the vulnerable `/users/{user_id}/saved-issues`: the only change is where the user id comes from. `selectinload` is explained in lesson 4.12.

### Admin-only routes: a role dependency

In `deps.py`, a dependency built on top of `CurrentUser`:

```python
def require_admin(user: CurrentUser) -> User:
    is_admin = user.role == "admin"
    if not is_admin:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, "Administrators only")
    return user


AdminUser = Annotated[User, Depends(require_admin)]
```

A route that takes `admin: AdminUser` is admin-only, with no check inside the route to forget. `routes/repos.py`:

```python
@router.post("", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED, response_model=RepoOut)
def add_repo(body: RepoCreate, admin: AdminUser, session: SessionDep, ...) -> JSONResponse:
    exists = session.scalar(select(Repo.id).where(Repo.full_name == body.full_name)) is not None
    if exists:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT, f"{body.full_name} is already tracked")
    ...
```

(The full version also handles idempotency keys, lesson 4.16.) Adding a repository only records it; indexing it is slow work for the background worker in Part 5.

```text
$ uv run pytest tests/test_api_auth.py tests/test_api_resources.py -v -k "idempotent_and_private or only_admins or cannot_change_the_role"
tests/test_api_auth.py::test_patch_cannot_change_the_role PASSED
tests/test_api_resources.py::test_only_admins_may_add_a_repository PASSED
tests/test_api_resources.py::test_saving_is_idempotent_and_private PASSED
======================= 3 passed, 29 deselected in 1.16s =======================
```

`-k` picks tests whose names match the expression.

## Attack it

The same script, against Atlas as built:

```text
== Atlas
Mallory reads user 26's saved issues -> 404 {"detail":"Not Found"}
Mallory PATCHes role=admin -> 422 role is now None
Mallory adds a repository -> 403 {"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"Administrators only","request_id":"4c91fc21c2584a63b669014c2afa0968"}}
```

- The IDOR route doesn't exist: there's no URL that names another user. (That 404 came back in FastAPI's default shape, not Atlas's: a real bug that lesson 4.14 fixes.)
- The PATCH is refused with 422 and "Extra inputs are not permitted"; nothing changed, so `role` isn't in the response at all.
- Without the role, adding a repository is 403.

Where a route *must* take an id that could belong to someone else, the defence moves into the query. Lesson 4.20's notes are the example: `PATCH /notes/{note_id}` looks the note up `WHERE id = :note_id AND user_id = :me`, so another user's note is "not found", and its test checks exactly that.

## Trade-offs: expressing permissions *(deep dive)*

| Approach | Example | Good until |
|---|---|---|
| Checks in each route | `if user.role != "admin": raise ...` | the third route forgets it |
| Dependencies (Atlas) | `admin: AdminUser`; owner in every query | rules depend on many attributes at once |
| A policy function | `can(user, "edit", note)` used everywhere | you need policies stored as data, editable without deploys |
| A policy engine (OPA, Cedar) | rules in their own language, checked by a service | small apps: one more system to run and learn |
| Postgres row-level security | the database itself filters rows by the current user | connection pooling and per-request database roles get complicated |

Atlas has two roles and owner-only data, so dependencies plus owner filters cover it. A sign it's time to move up a row: the same permission rule appearing, slightly differently, in several routes.

## Common mistakes

- **Taking the user id from the request** (`/users/{id}/...`, or `{"user_id": 7}` in a body) instead of from the token.
- **Checking ownership after loading**, in Python, in some routes and forgetting in others. Filter by owner in the query.
- **Copying request data onto models wholesale** (`for k, v in body.items(): setattr(...)`): mass assignment.
- **Ignoring unknown fields silently**: attacks and typos both look like success.
- **403 for private resources** that should be invisible: it confirms they exist.
- **401 when the user is known but not allowed**: that's 403.

## Check yourself

**1.** Mallory's token was valid in every request of the attack. Why didn't authentication stop her?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Authentication only established that she is Mallory, which was true. The vulnerable routes never asked whether *Mallory* may read user 22's data or change her own role. That's authorisation, a separate check that has to be made for every action.
:::

**2.** Atlas's `UserUpdate` already listed only `skills_profile`. Why change it to refuse extra fields?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Ignoring them was safe but silent: the attack and a client's typo both got 200, so neither was noticed. With `extra="forbid"` both get 422 naming the unexpected field, which helps honest clients and makes attack attempts visible (and, in lesson 4.15, logged).
:::

**3.** A logged-in non-admin calls `POST /repos`. Which status, and why not 401?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
403 Forbidden. The user is authenticated (Atlas knows who they are), just not allowed. 401 would mean the credentials are missing or invalid.
:::

## Exercise

Write a test, red first, that `DELETE /issues/{id}/saved` by one user doesn't remove another user's saved issue. Make it fail by changing the route's `where` to filter by `issue_id` only, then restore it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
def test_unsaving_only_affects_me(client: TestClient, session: Session) -> None:
    ids = store_numbers(session, [3])
    ada = sign_up(client, "ada@example.com")
    grace = sign_up(client, "grace@example.com")
    client.put(f"/issues/{ids[3]}/saved", headers=ada)

    client.delete(f"/issues/{ids[3]}/saved", headers=grace)

    assert [issue["number"] for issue in client.get("/users/me/saved-issues", headers=ada).json()] == [3]
```
With the filter on `issue_id` only, Grace's delete removes Ada's row and the test fails with `assert [] == [3]`. Not in the reference code.
:::

## Stretch

Add `GET /issues/{issue_id}/saved` that answers `{"saved": true}` or `{"saved": false}` for the signed-in user, in one query, test first.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from sqlalchemy import exists


@router.get("/{issue_id}/saved")
def is_saved(issue_id: int, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> dict[str, bool]:
    statement = select(
        exists().where(saved_issues.c.user_id == user.id, saved_issues.c.issue_id == issue_id)
    )
    return {"saved": bool(session.scalar(statement))}
```
`EXISTS` stops at the first match. The test: save as Ada, check Ada sees `true` and Grace sees `false`. Not in the reference code.
:::

## What changed in the project

`saved_issues` table; `require_admin` and `AdminUser` in `deps.py`; routes `PUT`/`DELETE /issues/{id}/saved`, `GET /users/me/saved-issues`, `GET`/`POST /repos`; request schemas refuse unknown fields. Commits: `feat: Added saved issues and admin-only repositories`, `fix: Refused request fields a schema doesn't list instead of silently ignoring them`.
